question: A US rule taxed Nike’s imports on the price of a similar American-made shoe, if one existed, and Nike’s duty soared. What did Nike do?
options: Moved all its production to America
Made a cheap similar shoe in Maine
Raised its own prices to match
answer: It made a cheap similar shoe in Maine. Nike launched One Line, a plain nylon running shoe built at its Saco factory and priced just above cost, so customs had a new, low American price to measure its imports against. Knight called the move ‘American Selling Price ourselves’; a settlement with customs followed in 1980.
move: When a rule is used against you, check whether it cuts both ways.
trap: ‘Moved all its production to America’: dodging the duty seems the obvious fix.
simply: If your bill is set by the price of a sandwich at the shop next door, and that shop keeps raising it, open your own stall and sell a cheap one.
why: Rules written for one purpose can often be met on their own terms. Before fighting a rule head-on, read exactly what it measures; sometimes changing the thing it measures is quicker than changing the rule.
reference: Phil Knight, Shoe Dog: A Memoir by the Creator of Nike (Scribner, 2016), chapters ‘1977’ and ‘1980’
